# Block 4: What the interval does not say {.unnumbered} *Roughly 25 minutes, and almost no code. This is the chapter that separates you from most of the people whose papers you will read.* ## Part A: the answer to the trap Interval number 4,271 either contains the true mean or it does not. There is no probability involved. The true mean is a fixed number. Your interval, once computed, is two fixed numbers. Either the fixed number lies between the two fixed numbers or it does not. The probability is 1 or it is 0, and you do not know which. This feels like a swindle. You did the work, you have an interval, and the answer to "how likely is it that I am right?" is *"either certainly yes or certainly no, and I decline to say which"*. It is not a swindle. It is the honest limit of what this machinery delivers. ## Part B: what it does say The 95% attaches to the **procedure**, not to your interval. > If you repeated the whole business ten thousand times, 95% of the intervals you built would contain the true mean. You built one. It came out of a process with a 95% hit rate. That is a fact about the process. Nothing whatever follows about your particular interval, in the same way that nothing follows about a particular coin flip from the fact that the coin is fair. Go back to @fig-coverage in Block 3 and cover the dashed line with your thumb. That is your situation. You can see your interval. You cannot see the truth. You have no way to tell whether yours is one of the 95 or one of the 5. ## Part C: the six statements Hoekstra and colleagues [@hoekstra2014] gave researchers and students a scenario: a 95% confidence interval running from 0.1 to 0.4. Then six statements, to be marked true or false. Mark each one before you read on. There is no penalty and nobody is watching. --- **1.** The probability that the true mean is greater than 0 is at least 95%. **2.** The probability that the true mean equals 0 is smaller than 5%. **3.** The null hypothesis that the true mean equals 0 is likely to be incorrect. **4.** There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies between 0.1 and 0.4. **5.** We can be 95% confident that the true mean lies between 0.1 and 0.4. **6.** If we were to repeat the experiment over and over, then 95% of the time the true mean falls between 0.1 and 0.4. ---
Every one of them assigns a probability to the **parameter**. The parameter has no probability. It is a fixed number. - **1, 2, 3** make claims about the true mean directly. They are posterior statements wearing a frequentist coat. - **4** is the one nearly everyone endorses. It is what you wanted to write in Block 3. It is a credible interval's statement, not a confidence interval's. - **5** looks safer because "confident" sounds vaguer than "probable". It is not. Either the word means something, in which case it is statement 4, or it means nothing, in which case do not write it. - **6** is the subtle one, and it catches people who believe they have understood. Read it carefully: it lets the **interval stay still** and the **true mean move about**. That is precisely backwards. The true mean is nailed down. The interval is what varies from experiment to experiment. Look at @fig-coverage again: the dashed line is the thing that does not move. The true statement, which is not on the list, is about the procedure: *if we repeat the experiment over and over, 95% of the intervals we construct will contain the true mean.*
:::{.callout-note} ## The results 120 researchers and 442 students, all in psychology. Both groups endorsed, on average, **more than three of the six** [@hoekstra2014]. Self-declared statistical experience did not predict performance. Researchers barely outperformed first-year students who had received no instruction in inference whatsoever. Lyu and colleagues [@lyu2020] surveyed 1,479 researchers and students across a range of fields and found the same pattern, with one addition: most respondents were **confident** in their incorrect answers. If you got several wrong, you are in the ordinary condition of a working scientist. The difference is that you now know. ::: ## Part D: why the wrong answer is so attractive Because statement 4 is what you actually want. You want to know about the world, given your data. The interval tells you about your data, given the world. Those are different conditional statements, and swapping them is not a slip of the tongue. It is a different question with a different answer. - **P(interval like mine | true mean is X)** is what you have. Frequentist inference is built entirely out of statements of this shape. - **P(true mean is X | interval like mine)** is what you want. It is not available. Not for want of cleverness. Because the second is a probability *about the parameter*, and in this framework parameters do not have probabilities. They are fixed, unknown constants. Asking for the probability that the mean is 0.52 g is, here, like asking for the probability that 7 is prime. **Which of these does a frequentist method give you?**
## Part E: so who is allowed to say statement 4? Somebody is. There is a framework in which *"there is a 95% probability the true mean lies between 0.1 and 0.4"* is a perfectly respectable sentence with a precise meaning. To get in, you have to pay an entry fee. The fee is the subject of Block 5. Your instinct was not stupid. It was a coherent statement in the wrong framework. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Three things to write down :::: ::::{.task-container} 1. **Which of the six did you endorse?** Write it down now, before you forget. It will be useful next week, when the p-value turns out to invite exactly the same error. 2. **Explain to somebody not on this module** why "95% confident" does not mean "95% probable". If you cannot do it in two sentences, you have not got it yet. 3. **Rewrite each of the six into something true.** Some need only a small change. At least one cannot be rescued at all, only deleted. Which, and why? :::: :::
Try the mechanical fix first: move the probability off the parameter and onto the procedure. So statement 4, "there is a 95% probability that the true mean lies between 0.1 and 0.4", becomes "this interval was produced by a procedure that captures the true mean 95% of the time". Notice what that costs you. The rewritten version says nothing about **your** interval at all. It is a true sentence about a method, offered in place of the false sentence about the world that you actually wanted. Every honest rewrite pays that price. Now try statement 3, "the null hypothesis is likely to be incorrect", with the same trick. It resists, because "likely" is doing the work and there is nowhere for it to go: the sentence is *entirely* a claim about the probability of a hypothesis. There is no procedure-flavoured version underneath it to salvage. It is not an imprecise sentence. It is a sentence from a different framework, and the only fix is to delete it or become a Bayesian.
